title: PostgreSQL: indexing & read performance
description: B-tree basics, composite, covering and partial indexes, plus GIN, JSONB, full-text search and PostGIS for the cases that replace extra systems.
source: Study notes: when and how to use PostgreSQL in system design interviews

questions.prompt: Which query shapes does the default B-tree index handle well?

options.text: Exact matches, range queries and sorting on the indexed column.
options.why: Right: these are B-tree strengths.

options.text: Only exact matches; ranges and ordering need another type.
options.why: B-trees keep keys ordered, so ranges and ORDER BY work.

options.text: Only full-text searches over very long documents.
options.why: Text search needs a GIN index over a tsvector.

options.text: Only queries that join more than three tables.
options.why: Joins are helped by indexes on join keys but are not the definition.

questions.explanation: B-tree is the default and your bread-and-butter index for equality, range and ordered reads.

questions.prompt: A candidate proposes an index on every column "to be safe". What is the best response?

options.text: Each index slows writes and uses disk, so index only for real query patterns.
options.why: Right: every index has a maintenance cost.

options.text: Agree, because extra indexes never affect performance negatively.
options.why: They slow inserts and updates because each must be maintained.

options.text: Agree, because the planner always uses every available index.
options.why: The planner may choose a sequential scan instead.

options.text: Reject indexes entirely, because the primary key is enough.
options.why: Other query patterns still need their own indexes.

questions.explanation: Indexes cost write speed, space and WAL volume, and may go unused. Add them for known access patterns.

questions.prompt: A profile page runs WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC. Which index fits best?

options.text: One index on (user_id, created_at).
options.why: Right: it finds the user rows and returns them already ordered.

options.text: Two separate single-column indexes on user_id and created_at.
options.why: The planner has to combine them and may still sort.

options.text: An index on created_at only.
options.why: It would scan all dates instead of jumping to one user.

options.text: No index, relying on the table's primary key.
options.why: The key is on id, which this query does not filter by.

questions.explanation: Put the equality column first and the sort column second so one index scan serves the whole query.

questions.prompt: Which feature lets PostgreSQL run full-text search on posts without Elasticsearch?

options.text: A tsvector column with a GIN index, queried with @@ to_tsquery.
options.why: Right: GIN maps words to the rows containing them.

options.text: A B-tree index on the content column with LIKE '%word%' as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: A leading wildcard cannot use a B-tree index.

options.text: A foreign key from posts to a separate words table in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Foreign keys enforce integrity; they do not search text.

options.text: A partial index that only covers deleted posts.
options.why: That helps a different problem and does not provide text search.

questions.explanation: GIN works like a book index. PostgreSQL search supports stemming, ranking, multiple languages and boolean queries.

questions.prompt: Select all requirements that suggest adding Elasticsearch instead of PostgreSQL search.

options.text: Faceted search and advanced relevancy scoring.
options.why: Yes: these are search-engine strengths.

options.text: Fuzzy matching and search-as-you-type experiences.
options.why: Yes: beyond what built-in search does comfortably.

options.text: Distributed search over a very large corpus.
options.why: Yes: that is where a dedicated cluster pays off.

options.text: Finding posts that contain two specific words.
options.why: Basic boolean text search is easily handled in PostgreSQL.

questions.explanation: Start with built-in search for simple needs; add Elasticsearch only when a requirement outgrows it.

questions.prompt: Posts carry varying attributes such as hashtags, mentions and media. How can PostgreSQL store and query them flexibly?

options.text: A JSONB column with a GIN index, queried using the @> operator.
options.why: Right: flexible shape plus indexed containment queries.

options.text: A new column added to the table for every possible attribute without any extra configuration.
options.why: That makes the schema sprawl and needs migrations.

options.text: A plain text column parsed by the application on each read.
options.why: The database cannot index or filter that efficiently.

options.text: A separate MongoDB cluster for the metadata only.
options.why: It adds a system the JSONB feature makes unnecessary.

questions.explanation: JSONB gives NoSQL-style flexibility inside PostgreSQL while keeping transactions and joins.

questions.prompt: You need posts within 5 km of a user. What is the PostgreSQL way?

options.text: The PostGIS extension with a GiST index and ST_DWithin.
options.why: Right: spatial types and indexed distance queries.

options.text: Two B-tree indexes on latitude and longitude with a LIKE filter.
options.why: That cannot efficiently express a distance radius.

options.text: A GIN index on a tsvector holding the place names.
options.why: Text search does not compute distances.

options.text: A trigger that copies each post to every nearby user.
options.why: That is fan-out, not a spatial query.

questions.explanation: PostGIS can serve many geo needs before a specialised database is needed. Uber once ran ride matching on it.

questions.prompt: What does INCLUDE (title, created_at) add to an index on user_id?

options.text: The query can be answered from the index alone, without fetching table rows.
options.why: Right: an index-only scan.

options.text: The index also enforces uniqueness for title and created_at in a typical production setup.
options.why: INCLUDE columns are payload, not part of the key.

options.text: The index becomes smaller and faster to update for most everyday workloads.
options.why: It becomes larger and costs slightly more on writes.

options.text: The table no longer needs a primary key.
options.why: The primary key requirement is unrelated.

questions.explanation: Covering indexes trade space and write cost for fewer heap lookups on hot read queries.

questions.prompt: Most queries target active users but many rows are soft-deleted. Which index idea helps?

options.text: A partial index with WHERE status = 'active'.
options.why: Right: smaller and cheaper to maintain.

options.text: A full index on status alone.
options.why: It indexes everything including the rows you never query.

options.text: A unique index that includes the deleted rows.
options.why: That grows the index and does not target the hot subset.

options.text: Deleting the index whenever a row is soft-deleted.
options.why: Rebuilding indexes per row would be wildly expensive.

questions.explanation: Index only the subset you query. Smaller indexes fit in memory and speed both reads and writes.
